Female Waterbuck calves typically weigh around 13.6 kilograms [Wwb = around 13.6 kilograms] at birth, a neonatal mass that is relatively substantial for a bovid of this size and provides the newborn with a degree of precocial capacity crucial for avoiding predators in the dense riparian habitats they frequent. Gestation in this species has been documented to last approximately 264 days [tg = approximately 264 days] under the standard thermoneutral body temperature of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C], a period that aligns with expectations for a large-bodied antelope and reflects the considerable investment in producing a single, well-developed calf per litter [N_R_i = single, well-developed calf per litter]. The timing of reproductive events is tightly constrained by seasonal resource availability, and females typically produce only one litter annually [F_R_i = one litter annually].

As female calves mature, they experience a prolonged dependency period before achieving nutritional independence. Weaning, defined as the cessation of milk intake and the transition to a fully herbivorous diet, occurs at approximately 213 days after birth [tx = approximately 213 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This extended suckling period is characteristic of the tribe Reduncini, allowing the young to develop a functional rumen and acquire the necessary gut microflora for digesting coarse grasses. During this time, the mother and calf form a close bond, with the calf remaining hidden in dense vegetation for the first several weeks of life, a classic "hider" strategy that minimizes predation risk. The considerable energetic demands of lactation on the dam are thus concentrated into a period of roughly seven months, after which the now-weaned juvenile must rely entirely on its own foraging success to sustain growth and development through the subsequent sub-adult phase.

The attainment of sexual maturity in female Waterbuck marks a significant life-history transition, occurring relatively late compared to many other African ungulates. Field data indicate that puberty is reached at approximately 771 days after birth [tp = approximately 771 days after birth] under the species' typical core body temperature of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This protracted time to maturity, spanning over two years, reflects the substantial somatic investment required for females to reach a body size sufficient to support the energetic costs of gestation and lactation. Delayed first reproduction is a common pattern in larger ungulates, as it allows females to continue growing and accumulating fat reserves, which are critical for successfully rearing a calf in the face of seasonal nutritional bottlenecks. The extended juvenile period also provides ample time for learning complex social behaviors and establishing a home range within a female-dominated herd structure.

Adult body mass in Waterbuck exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a direct consequence of the polygynous mating system where males compete intensely for access to receptive females. Females typically attain an ultimate wet weight in the range of 161 to 214 kilograms (161-214 kilograms) [Wwi = 161-214 kilograms], with a central estimate often cited around 185 kilograms. Males, in contrast, are considerably heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight that commonly falls between 198 and 262 kilograms (198-262 kilograms) [Wwi = 198-262 kilograms], with a representative figure of roughly 230 kilograms. This substantial divergence in mass is driven by intrasexual selection favoring larger body size in males, which confers an advantage in the often-violent dominance interactions that determine mating access. The ecological consequence of this dimorphism is a differentiation in forage selection and habitat use, with males often exploiting slightly different grassland niches to meet their greater absolute metabolic demands.

The maximum recorded lifespan for Waterbuck in a natural setting is approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when measured against the background of their typical active metabolism at 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a medium-to-large antelope and suggests that individuals, once they reach adulthood, face relatively low rates of extrinsic mortality from predation, likely due to their large body size and the protective nature of their preferred habitat along permanent watercourses. As animals approach the end of their natural lifespan, signs of physiological senescence become apparent, including dental wear that reduces foraging efficiency and a decline in overall body condition. This eventual physical deterioration, combined with increased vulnerability to predators and disease, ultimately leads to natural mortality, completing a life cycle that is finely tuned to the dynamic floodplain ecosystems of sub-Saharan Africa.
